title: Give Objects Behavior
content:
What problem does this solve?
Objects become useful when related behavior can live beside their state. A method is a function defined on a class. When you call `player.heal(2)`, that player is passed to the method as self.

Read state
A method can use self attributes to calculate and return information without changing the object.

Change state
A method can also assign a new value to `self.attribute`, creating a state transition on that particular object.

Behavior belongs where responsibility belongs
Learning classes does not mean every function should become a method. A calculation involving two unrelated numbers may remain a free function. A behavior that naturally acts on one object's state is a stronger method candidate.

Vocabulary after the behavior
An instance method is behavior called through an instance. State is the data currently stored on an object; a state transition is a deliberate change to that data.
concepts: Methods are functions attached to classes and called through objects
self is the instance before the dot in a method call
Methods can read state without changing it
Methods can update self attributes to change one object
Not every helper needs to become a method

examples.title: Read state
examples.explanation: The method reads object state and returns a calculation without mutation.

examples.title: Change state
examples.explanation: The method updates this instance through self.value.

common_mistakes: Forgetting self in a method signature
Forgetting parentheses when a method call is required
Updating a local variable instead of self.attribute
Returning the old state before applying an update
Putting unrelated utility behavior into a class only because classes exist
Assuming every method must mutate state

exercises.title: Read state through a method
hints: b becomes self for the doubled call.
The method reads b.value, which is 3, and multiplies it by 2.
The output is 6.

exercises.title: Change the object
exercises.prompt: Complete `add_one` so it changes this Counter instance from value to value + 1.
hints: The value to change lives on the current instance.
Use the same self attribute on both sides of the assignment.
Assign `self.value = self.value + 1`.

exercises.title: State after two calls
hints: Track the same c object through both calls.
Each call adds 1 to the existing self.value.
0 becomes 1, then 2.

exercises.title: Method or free helper?
exercises.prompt: A calculation only needs two unrelated numbers and no object state. Must it become a method now that classes exist?
choices: Yes; all new functions should be methods.
No; an ordinary function may be clearer when no object owns the behavior.
hints: Ask what object state the calculation naturally belongs to.
If no object owns the inputs or result, attaching it to a class adds ceremony without responsibility.
A free function may be clearer.

exercises.title: Update the attribute, not a local
exercises.prompt: Repair `take_damage` so it changes `self.health` and returns the new health.
hints: The health that persists between calls is stored on the object.
Read and write self.health, not an undefined/local health name.
Use `self.health = self.health - amount` and return self.health.

exercises.title: Damage and heal
exercises.prompt: Add `take_damage(amount)` and `heal(amount)` to Character. Each method changes `self.health` by the amount and returns the new health. Do not clamp health; zero and negative results are allowed by this Python exercise.
hints: Both methods update the same self.health attribute in opposite arithmetic directions.
Damage subtracts amount; heal adds amount; return the updated attribute after assignment.
Implement both methods with `self.health = self.health ± amount`, then return self.health.

exercises.title: Inventory behavior
exercises.prompt: Add `add_item(item)` that appends to `self.inventory`, and `item_count()` that returns `len(self.inventory)`.
hints: add_item should change the persistent inventory list on this instance.
item_count only reads state and returns len(self.inventory).
Append item through self.inventory; define a second method returning its length.

exercises.title: Character Behavior Check
exercises.prompt: Build `Character(name, health)` with a fresh inventory and methods `take_damage`, `heal`, `add_item`, and `summary`. `summary()` returns exactly `name`, `health`, and `item_count`. Hidden checks exercise multiple method calls on separate instances and verify one character never changes the other.
hints: Set up all persistent state in __init__ first, especially a fresh inventory list.
Each mutating method changes only self; summary should read the final state rather than duplicate stored counts.
Use take_damage/heal on self.health, append through self.inventory, and return a dictionary using len(self.inventory).

tests.expression: (lambda pair: pair[0].inventory is not pair[1].inventory)([Character("A",1), Character("B",1)])

exercises.success_message: The class now owns both state and related behavior, while separate instances remain independent.
